name: Virtual temperature
seoDesc: Virtual temperature: work out station pressure from the air temperature and the vapor pressure. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary: Give the Virtual temperature calculator the air temperature, the vapor pressure, the mixing ratio and the virtual temperature and it returns station pressure. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Virtual temperature calculator work?
sections.html:
The Virtual temperature calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports station pressure in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the method); then you type in the air temperature, the vapor pressure, the mixing ratio and the virtual temperature.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as use temperatures and use mixing ratio. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in hectopascals. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in g/kg.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Virtual temperature calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Station pressure=-379 × vapor pressure × virtual temperature ÷ (1000 × air temperature − 1000 × virtual temperature)
Dew point=-2373 × exponent ÷ (10 × exponent − 75)
Exponent=the natural log of ((100 ÷ 611) × vapor pressure) ÷ the natural log of (10)
Air temperature=100000 × virtual temperature ÷ (61 × mixing ratio + 100000)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Method set to Use temperatures, Air temperature = 10 °C, Vapor pressure = 10 hPa and Virtual temperature = 10 °C. Working through the relationship above gives Dew point = 178 °C and Exponent = 3.214.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Dew point = 178 °C and Exponent = 3.214 should be roughly the size you expected from Method set to Use temperatures and Air temperature = 10 °C.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Virtual temperature calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the air temperature, the vapor pressure and the mixing ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Virtual temperature calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns station pressure, derived from the air temperature, the vapor pressure and the mixing ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Virtual temperature calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the air temperature, the vapor pressure, the mixing ratio and the virtual temperature, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter air temperature in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Air temperature opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Dew point = 178 °C. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Virtual temperature calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
